session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Participants will be framed as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the specific places they go, the food they eat, the company they keep. The collective identity is 'men in the UK thinking about how they live day-to-day', not researchers or experts on masculinity. I will avoid framing them as people with opinions on gender theory and instead keep the anchor concrete: what they actually do, eat, and experience.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or defensively dismissive answers ('gender doesn't affect what I eat'). Will require behavioural grounding early — getting to specific moments and past events rather than general attitudes.

Social acceptability of plant-based foods (Sections 4–5): Risk of consensus hardening quickly around practical/cost barriers, masking deeper identity and social concerns. Will need sharpening moves and dissent invitations.

The relationship between masculine identity and food: Participants may hold implicit associations between meat and masculinity without being able to name them directly. Contradictions between stated positions and described behaviours are the most valuable data here — must track carefully.

What would actually need to change for plant-based eating to be viable (Section 4): Risk of abstract or aspirational answers. Need to keep this grounded in real constraints — social, practical, emotional — not just stated preferences.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Unknown from profile alone — 45, suburban South East. May be relatively comfortable in group settings given age and context, but no strong prior anticipation.

48, suburban East of England. Oldest of the group by a small margin. May be more settled in his views; could either anchor the group or resist novelty. Worth watching for early opinion-leadership signals.

45, suburban South West. No distinguishing profile markers. Monitor for early reticence — South West context sometimes associated with more traditional attitudes that could feel less speakable in a group.

40, suburban North West. Youngest of the group by 5 years. May hold somewhat different reference points from the others. Worth tracking whether he self-positions as different from the older participants.
47, suburban South East — same region as Andrew. Possible rapport between them if they pick up on that. No other distinguishing markers.

known_risk_conditions: Topic produces socially desirable answers by design — men discussing gender and food choices are likely to present themselves as more flexible or enlightened than their actual behaviour. Behavioural grounding (specific past events, real meals, named occasions) is essential from Section 2 onward.

Consensus risk is structurally high in an all-male group on a topic that touches masculine identity — participants may align around a shared 'laddish pragmatism' frame that masks real diversity. Must watch for premature convergence, especially in Sections 3–5.

The word 'gender' (Section 3 scripted question) may trigger a defensive or intellectualised response. If participants pivot to abstract gender-theory language or blanket dismissal ('no, I just eat what I fancy'), will need a quick behavioural redirect without leading.

Plant-based eating carries active stigma in some male social contexts — participants may perform indifference or mild hostility for social reasons rather than expressing genuine attitudes. Indirect probing (social context, what others think, specific scenarios) will be more useful than direct attitude questions.
Group is entirely suburban UK men in their 40s — high homogeneity increases conformity risk. Need to work harder to surface genuine diversity of experience than with a mixed-profile group.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro, opening context): Very light touch. The goal is rapport and getting voices in the room. Minimal probing — enough to hear from everyone, not enough to exhaust the warmup topics. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): Moderate directivity. Begin transitioning from general attitudes to specific behaviours. Introduce behavioural grounding here so the norm is established before we hit the sensitive sections. Sections 3–5 (main topics): Highest directivity. Active use of contradictions, dissent invitations, and behavioural probes. Do not let abstract answers stand unchallenged. Use sharpening moves when consensus forms too quickly. Section 6 (closing): Very light. Offer space for addition but do not reopen closed topics or probe for depth.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the core research weight and receive the largest share combined (~55% of total budget). Context sections (1, 2) serve as warm-up and behavioural grounding and receive a moderate share (~30%). Intro and closing are functional bookends and receive minimal budget (~15% combined).

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — participants established geographic and occupational identity (construction, electrical, HR, work-from-home) and briefly signalled life-stage differences around family and commuting. A spontaneous theme of work-life balance emerged organically across several introductions, with participants triangulating their own situations against each other's. No substantive topic has yet been explored; the section functioned as social orientation rather than thematic discussion.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator kept the opening brief and low-stakes, using a round-robin geography prompt to get everyone speaking early. The spontaneous balance thread that emerged was noted but sensibly not pursued — the moderator redirected cleanly into the first substantive question. Allowing participants to self-introduce without interruption worked well; all four spoke voluntarily and unprompted, suggesting a comfortable early group dynamic.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on leisure time and socialising, with life-stage and work-type emerging as the dominant structuring forces. A productive contrast developed between physical and mental fatigue as drivers of different unwinding styles, while a deeper tension surfaced around freedom versus constraint — those without domestic responsibilities describing expansive, self-directed time, and those with young families or home-working arrangements describing compressed, fitted-in socialising. Notably, Nick reframed constraint as focus rather than deprivation, complicating a simple freedom/restriction binary.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator largely let Andrew and John's organic exchange run, intervening only when it risked excluding the remaining three. Direct address to Paul successfully retrieved a quiet voice. The section transition felt clean and timely — the life-stage theme had reached a natural resolution in Nick and Paul's contributions. Allowing participant-to-participant dialogue to develop the mental/physical fatigue distinction worked well; the moderator's light touch preserved authenticity without losing direction.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Sarah, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it's going to be recorded for research purposes, so just bear that in mind. The most important thing I'd say going in is: don't overthink it. There genuinely are no right or wrong answers here — we're interested in what you actually think and do, not what sounds like the correct thing to say. It's a conversation, not an interview, so if something someone else says connects with your experience, just jump in — you don't need to wait to be asked. And equally, if your experience is completely different from what someone else is describing, that's just as useful to us. So — just be yourselves, be respectful of each other, and keep things reasonably brief where you can so everyone gets a chance to speak. Right, let's get started. Let's go round and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
Right, I'm John. I'm from down in the South West, suburban area. Been here quite a while now, so it's home really. That's about it from me.

I'm Nick. North West, suburban as well so I'm kind of in the same boat as John there. I work in electrical and electronics, so I'm out on the road most days installing stuff, travelling between different sites. Got a wife, a young kid at home, and yeah — trying to keep all that balanced really. That's me.

I'm Paul, South East, suburban like you Nick. Yeah, I get what you mean about the balance thing. I work from home though, so it's a bit different — no commute, which helps. But I'm in HR and training, supporting people through recruitment and that sort of stuff. So it's still juggling work and home, just without the travel element you've got. My wife and I, no kids at home, so I suppose we've got it a bit easier than you in that respect. But yeah, South East suburban crew here as well.

Yeah, I'm Daniel, East of England — suburban area like you lot. And I hear what you're saying, Nick. I'm in construction, building finishing work mostly, so I'm out on sites all over the region pretty much every day. Not quite as far afield as you might be, but still driving around, different locations all the time. 

The balance thing — yeah, that resonates. My wife's working too, so it's not like one of us is holding the fort at home. We've got the house sorted, no kids living with us anymore, which I suppose makes it easier than what Nick's dealing with. But it's still that juggling act of early starts, getting back in the evening, trying to keep on top of things at home. Different from Paul's setup where he's at least there during the day.

Great, thanks everyone — good to know who's in the room. So we've got construction, electrical, HR, and a mix of family setups across the South East, South West, North West, and East of England. Right, let's get into it. First question — and feel free to be as specific as you like here — what's your favourite place in your city or town to spend time with your male friends? Could be a pub, a sports ground, someone's garage, anywhere really. What do you lot actually do?

Right, yeah, I'm Andrew. South East as well, suburban. I work in logistics and transport — management side of things — so bit different from you lot maybe, but also covering a lot of ground during the week. No kids here though, live on my own actually, so that's... that's my situation.

But to your question, Sarah — honestly, the pub's the main one for me. There's a couple we tend to go to round here. One's just walking distance from where I live, so that's handy on a Friday or Saturday evening. Nothing fancy, just a decent local where you can actually hear people talk, you know? Not one of those places where the music's so loud you're basically lip-reading your mates.

And then — this might sound a bit different from what you're all describing — but I do quite a bit with the lads at weekends driving out, actually. Bit of a car thing really. We'll head out to the coast or drive up to see some mates further afield, stop at a pub somewhere different. That sort of thing. So it's not always the same place, but for me it's more about having the time to get out and do something, rather than being stuck locally. 

With the commute and work, by the time Friday comes round I'm ready to get in the car and go somewhere, if that makes sense.

Yeah, I get that completely, Andrew. I'm the same — by Friday you just want to get away from it, don't you. We've got some decent routes down here, coastal stuff especially. I'll head out that way when I can, bit of a drive, clear your head. Nothing organised really, just grab the van sometimes and head out, maybe stop somewhere different. You're right about the pub thing too though — there's a couple of decent locals I'll go to, but honestly with the hours I'm doing most weeks I'm knackered by the time the weekend comes. So a lot of it ends up being work on the van, bit of tinkering in the driveway, and then yeah, if the weather's decent or I've got the energy, get out for a drive. But the pub's not really a regular thing for me, not like it sounds like it is for you. Just depends how I'm feeling really.

Yeah, that's fair. I mean, I think there's a difference though, isn't there — like, I'm sat at a desk most of the time, managing people, dealing with paperwork and all that. So by Friday I'm tired, but it's more... mental, I suppose. Whereas you're doing physical work on the van, out on your feet all day, so that's a different kind of knackered. I can understand why you'd just want to tinker on the driveway rather than go out somewhere.

For me it's more that I need to move, get out of the house, change of scenery. But I get what you're saying — some weeks I wake up Saturday morning and think, right, I could either drag myself to the pub or just stay in and do some stuff around the place. It depends on the week I've had really.

The van thing though — that's interesting. Do you get mates round to help with that, or is that more of a solo thing for you?

Nah, mostly solo to be honest. I mean, there's the other person in the house, but he's not really into that sort of thing. So it's just me pottering about, you know — oils, filters, bit of maintenance, whatever needs doing. Keeps the van running properly, saves money on the garage bills. I quite like it actually, just having something to do with your hands when you've been sitting down all week. It's different from what you're saying though — you're right about that. I'm physically tired, yeah, but that's the kind of tired where you still want to do something, just... quieter, I suppose. Out there in the driveway, not having to think too much about it. Whereas what you're describing, that mental fatigue thing, I can see why you'd want to get out and be around people, change it up completely. Different ways of unwinding really, aren't they.

That distinction between the two types of tiredness is interesting — sounds like it shapes quite a lot. Daniel, Nick, Paul — what about you lot? Where do you tend to end up when you're spending time with your mates?

Yeah, so for me it's the pub, to be honest. There's a couple of regulars I go to round here, nothing special — just local spots where you know the landlord, see the same faces. Friday nights mostly, sometimes a Saturday if it's been a decent week. 

But it's not just that I'm sitting there for hours or anything. It's more that you get a pint, have a chat with the lads, bit of banter about what's been going on. Work, football, whatever. Nothing heavy. I think with the building sites, you're around people all day anyway — dealing with the lads on the crew, supervisory stuff — so the pub's different, isn't it. It's the same blokes you might know from years back, not your work mates. Just easier somehow.

I get what Andrew's saying about needing to get out and move around, and I get John's thing about the tinkering too — I do bits on the house and the van at weekends. But the pub's where I actually spend time with mates properly. It's close to home, we know it, it's just straightforward. Don't have to think about it.

Right, yeah — I hear what you're all saying, but it's a bit different for me, to be honest. I mean, I do want to get out and move around like Andrew, and I get the whole tinkering thing John's on about — I'm into that, actually, bit of home automation stuff, wiring projects, that sort of thing. But by the time the weekend comes round, most of my time's taken up with the family really. My kid's under five, so it's parks, soft play, visiting relatives, that kind of stuff. And then there's work on the house that needs doing, garden bits.

I don't really get much time down the pub with the lads like you lot are describing. Not regularly anyway. I mean, sometimes I might manage an hour or so, but you've got to get back, haven't you. The wife needs a break too. It's not the same as being able to just head out for the evening or drive somewhere on a whim like Andrew's doing.

So I suppose for me it's more... snatched time really. Bit of tinkering in the garage between other stuff, catching up with someone when I can. Different setup to what you're all describing, but yeah — that's the reality of it at the minute.

Yeah, that's... that's quite a shift, isn't it Nick. I mean, we're all talking about getting out, or tinkering, or a regular Friday night down the pub, and you're basically fitting in bits around everything else. That's a different thing altogether.

I think — and I don't want to sound like I'm oversimplifying it — but not having kids at home, that's a massive difference. I can just decide on a Friday, right, I'm going to head out, spend the evening with the lads, not worry about it. Whereas you're... you're constantly juggling, aren't you. Even when you do get to the garage or whatever, it's never quite your own time because you know there's other stuff waiting.

I mean, I've got mates with young kids, and I see it — they're always checking their phone, they've got to get back. You can't just lose an evening. So when you do manage to get that hour down the pub, it's probably more... I dunno, compressed somehow? More valuable but also a bit stressful because you know the clock's ticking?

It does make you appreciate what Daniel's talking about actually — just being able to go to the same pub, same time, same blokes. That consistency, when you've got it. Not sure that's possible for you right now, is it?

Yeah, no, you're right that it's different. And yeah, the clock's ticking, but honestly — I'm not sure I'm missing out as much as it sounds like I should be. I mean, don't get me wrong, I'd like more time sometimes, but that compressed thing you're talking about? That actually works for me.

When I do get an hour in the garage or manage to meet someone for a quick pint, I'm actually there, you know. Not sat half-engaged nursing a beer, thinking about what else is on. It's focused. And maybe that sounds like I'm making the best of a bad situation or whatever, but it's not really how I see it. It's just how it is right now, and it's fine.

The consistency thing — yeah, that would be nice sometimes. But I don't know if I need it the way you're describing it. I've got what's happening at home, which is its own thing entirely. It's not like I'm pining for a regular Friday night down the pub that I'm missing out on. That's not really where my head's at.

I think maybe it just depends what stage you're in, doesn't it. You've got that freedom, which is great for what you want to do. I've got something else going on. Not better or worse, just... different.
Paul, you've been quiet — what about you, where do you tend to end up with your mates?

Yeah, fair point. I mean, I'm probably somewhere in between you lot, really. The pub, yeah — there's a couple of locals I'll go to, nothing fancy. But honestly it's not a massive part of my week. My wife and I, we tend to do a fair bit together, so some Friday nights we'll just stay in, maybe have people round instead. That feels easier than heading out somewhere, especially if we're both working through the day.

But I do get what you're all saying about needing to get out and decompress. I work from home, so I'm here all day anyway. I think that changes things for me — I'm not desperate to get away from the office or anything because I've already been here. So weekends tend to be a mix of sorting the house, bit of gardening, maybe a walk round the local green spaces. I do catch up with people, but it's more... organic, I suppose. Not a fixed Friday night thing like Daniel's describing.

I can see the appeal of that consistency though. But like you said, Nick — it's just different stages, isn't it. Right now that works for me.

Cheers Paul. So between you there's quite a mix — regular local for Daniel, heading out and driving for Andrew, tinkering on the van for John, fitting it in around family for Nick, more homeside and organic for Paul. Good stuff. Let's shift gears a bit — I want to ask about food. How do you all decide what to eat? Day to day, week to week — what's actually driving those choices for you?

Right, yeah — food. For me it's pretty straightforward really. When I'm on site, I'm usually up early, grab something quick at home or bring something with me. Sandwich, bit of fruit, flask of tea. Just whatever's practical because you're working, you're not sitting down for lunch properly most days. You've got maybe twenty minutes, and you're eating in the van or at the site.

Then when I get back in the evening, my wife's usually on her own routine too, so it depends what she's got on. We'll sort something out — bit of planning there, I suppose, some weeks she'll do a shop and we'll know roughly what we're cooking. Other weeks it's more... whatever we can throw together that doesn't take too long. Depends if we're both knackered or if one of us has got a bit more energy.

I don't really think about it much to be honest. It's fuel, isn't it. You need to eat because you're working physical jobs, travelling around. You can't do the work on an empty stomach. So it's just — what's quick, what fits round the day, what we've got in the kitchen. Nothing fancy. Not like you lot might be planning things out as much, with more time maybe. It's got to work round the sites and the driving.

Yeah, I mean — I get that, Daniel. The practicality side of it. But I think for us it's actually a bit different. My wife and I, we've kind of made a deliberate thing of it, especially since I'm working from home. It's not just fuel, if that makes sense.

We'll plan out the week a bit, actually sit down and think about what we fancy, what's in the cupboard. And then there's the cooking itself — we'll often do it together, bit of time in the evening when we can actually talk through the day, have a glass of wine, that kind of thing. It's become more of... I dunno, a ritual almost.

I suppose because we've both got the time a bit more than you're describing — you're knackered, you need something quick — we can afford to make it a bit more intentional. It's not wasted time for us, it's actually quite nice. And honestly, the food's better when you're not just grabbing whatever's easiest.

But I can see your point too — when you're coming in from a long day on site, the last thing you want is to be faffing about with a complicated meal. That's just not practical.

Yeah, fair enough. I mean, that sounds nice what you're doing — the planning bit, cooking together, all that. And I get it, if you've both got the time and you're here during the day anyway, you can think about it more. That makes sense.

But I wouldn't say it's just about being knackered and grabbing whatever's easiest, you know. My wife and we — we do think about what we're eating. We're not just shoving anything in. It's just... it works differently because of how the days go. I'm not sat at a desk here in the house all day, so I can't be popping home at half three thinking about what's for dinner. I'm miles away on a site somewhere.

And actually, when we do get time together at the weekend or whatever, we'll cook something decent. It's just not every night because there's not the space for it in the week. That doesn't make it less intentional though, does it. It's just got different constraints. We've still got to eat properly, we're still thinking about it — it's just that the ritual side of it isn't really there because of how work is set up.

So yeah, what you're describing sounds good, but it's not like one way's more thoughtful than the other. It's just different setups.

No, you're right. I didn't mean to make it sound like one's better than the other — that came across wrong. You're absolutely right, you're still thinking about it, you're still making sure you're eating properly. It's just the setup's different, like you said.

I suppose what I was trying to say badly is that we've got the luxury of time to make it a bit of an event, whereas you've got actual constraints that make that difficult. But that doesn't mean you're not being thoughtful about it. You're just working around what actually fits your day, which is fair enough.

And actually, doing something decent at the weekend when you've both got a bit more space — that's still the same thing, isn't it. You're still planning, still putting the effort in. Just compressed into a different time. So yeah, fair point.
That's a good distinction — different setups, same underlying thought going into it. Andrew, John, Nick — what does it look like for you? How do you tend to decide what you're eating?

Right, yeah — for me it's... it's a bit different again, I think. I mean, I live on my own, so there's no negotiating it with someone else or planning round another person's schedule. That's actually quite liberating in one way, but it also means it's entirely on me, which can go either direction.

During the week, honestly, it's fairly functional. I'm commuting, I'm at work early, I'm tired by the time I get back — bit like what you're saying, Daniel. I'll grab something quick, bit of meal prep on a Sunday sometimes if I can be bothered. But I'm not sitting down thinking about it much. It's just — what's in the fridge, what can I do in twenty minutes.

But then at the weekends, or if I've got a bit more energy, I'll actually cook something. And it's not because I'm doing it with anyone else like Paul and his wife — it's more for myself, just because I enjoy it actually. When I'm not knackered I quite like getting in the kitchen, trying something different. It's a bit of a break from work, proper focus on something.

The thing is though — living alone — there's no structure to it at all really. Some weeks I'm quite disciplined about it, other weeks it's just... whatever's easiest. There's no one else depending on you to have eaten properly, so you can kind of let it slide a bit if you're not in the mood. Which sounds a bit daft when I say it out loud, but that's honestly how it works.
